# Independent audit: all positive-right-index knot deficits

Source: `candidate 08dc040bda1a0f7a`.


stated double knot with d>=2 and J>=1. The remaining J=0 family is
not covered by this theorem. The sums are over h=0,1,2,...; stating
this explicitly in the theorem would remove a minor notational ambiguity.

I independently checked the following parts before consulting the exact
finite verifier.

1. Substituting the double-knot values gives
   v=(d+1)(H-J)/[d(H+J+1)]. The upper condition on H is precisely
   v<=1. The left endpoint is 1/(d+1-dv)=aH. The right endpoint is
   (1-dav)/(d+1+dv)=aJ. Both are exact mesh points. The q and p
   normalization in equation (2) retains the extra shift in p_h.

2. The infinite-mesh trapezoid identity has error (1/a) times the integral
   of the cell kernel (x-left)(right-x)/2 against the derivative variation.
   Its bound is a/8 times that variation. For the mass kernel the variation
   is d. The left kernel is convex on its active support and remains
   convex after its upward final derivative jump. The right kernel is
   concave only on its active interval; terminating exactly at aJ makes
   the finite-interval concave estimate valid without a last partial cell.

3. The right derivative drop is exactly
   (d-1)v C^(d-2)A+B(Q^(d-1)-C^(d-1)). Since Q-C=vA/B, the integer-power
   mean-value bound makes this at most 2(d-1)v A Q^(d-2). The claimed
   Q<=1+2/(3d) and Q^(d-2)<2 are correct, including d=2 and v=0.
   Thus the quadrature loss is at most b/2 with the stated constants.

4. Direct differentiation gives partial_s R=partial_x R+(d+1)T^(d-1),
   where T=1+sv+vx. The moving endpoint contributes zero because R
   vanishes there. Integration gives equation (8) with divisor d v.
   Bernoulli supplies a LOWER bound on that positive power difference,
   which is the needed orientation. The prefactor C_s^(d-1)A_s decreases
   from one with derivative -v C_s^(d-2)(1+d^2sv), and stays positive
   because A_s>=2/3. Therefore I(a,v)>=I(0,v)-av/(1+v) is an exact
   finite-shift inequality, not a first-order replacement.

5. To check the application of the separately audited Padé theorem, let
   f(v)=(1+v)^(d+1)/(1+theta v)^d. Direct integration gives, for v!=0,

       integral R_(0,v)=[f(v)-1-(1+theta)v]/(d v^2),
       integral L_v=[f(-v)-1+(1+theta)v]/(d v^2).

   Their sum is exactly the normalized expression in the Padé theorem.
   At v=0 both kernels have integral 1/[2(d+1)], so the limiting formula
   is valid there too. This proves the displayed continuous-gain bound
   with no missing factor of d or d+1.

6. The endpoint inequality R(0)>=(1+b/2)(1-b) multiplies Bernoulli
   by a positive factor, since b<=1/3. The resulting total positive
   contributions in the deficit are 3b/4+b^2/4+da/8. The exact knot
   identities give b<=v/(1+2v) and da<=1/(1+2v), both by increasing
   theta to one and decreasing J to one. The negative integral gain
   uses the lower bound 1/[a(d+1)]>=1+(4/3)v. These substitutions
   all go in the proper upper-bound direction and produce exactly U(v).

7. The cleared polynomial has the displayed coefficients. Each of the
   three stated Bernstein expansions is a polynomial identity with
   nonnegative basis functions summing to one. Every coefficient is
   at least 2/5, including the small middle-interval coefficient
   2071/5000>2/5. The denominator is at most 432, yielding precisely
   (2/5)/432=1/1080.

The exact verifier `supporting computation verify_positive_right_index_knot_theorem_minkowski.py`
was rerun and passed 9414 rational identities, quadrature bounds, and
certificate checks. Those checks support the algebra; the all-dimensional
conclusion rests on the analytic inequalities and finite polynomial
certificate just audited, not on a finite screen.
